frying_pan.hint: A wok is even better here — keep it screaming hot and toss instead of stirring.

gas_stove.hint: Induction works; heat the pan dry for a full minute first so the rice sears instead of sweating.

steps: Day-old rice is the whole game. Spread 2 cups on a plate and break the clumps apart with wet hands — freshly cooked rice steams instead of frying.
Beat 2 eggs with a pinch of salt. Slice 2 scallions, keeping the whites and greens apart.
Heat 1 tbsp oil in a wide pan over high heat until it shimmers. Add the eggs, scramble 20 seconds, and pull them out while still glossy.

Add another tbsp of oil and the scallion whites, fry 15 seconds, then add the rice. Press it flat against the pan for 30 seconds before stirring — that dry contact is what makes it taste fried rather than steamed.
Return the eggs, season with 1/2 tsp salt and a splash of light soy sauce, toss 30 seconds, and finish with the scallion greens.

dried_chili.hint: No dried chilies? Swap in 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes with a pinch of black pepper.

wok.hint: No wok? Use a large skillet over the highest heat your stove gives — work in two batches so the chicken sears instead of steaming.

steps: Cut the chicken into 3/4-inch cubes. Toss with 1 tsp cornstarch and 1 tsp light soy sauce, then rest for 10 minutes.
Mix the sauce in a small bowl: 1 tbsp light soy sauce, 1 tsp dark soy sauce (optional), 1 tbsp Chinkiang vinegar, 1 tsp sugar, 1 tsp cornstarch.
Heat 1 tbsp oil until it shimmers. Add the chicken in a single layer and let it sit untouched for 90 seconds before stirring.
Push the chicken to one side, add garlic and dried chilies to the oil, and fry for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Pour in the sauce and stir for 1 minute until it thickens and coats the chicken. Finish with scallion. Serve hot with rice.

frying_pan.hint: A wok works too — just keep the heat slightly lower so the eggs don't catch.

gas_stove.hint: An induction cooktop works fine; give the pan an extra minute to come up to temperature.

steps: Beat 3 eggs with a pinch of salt. Cut 2 tomatoes into wedges.
Heat 1 tbsp oil over medium-high. Pour in the eggs and wait 10 seconds, then fold gently until just set. Remove and set aside.
Add the tomatoes to the dry pan. Cook 3–4 minutes until they collapse and release their juice.
Add 1/2 tsp sugar (this is what balances the acidity — don't skip it) and 1/4 tsp salt.
Return the eggs, fold once or twice to combine, and serve immediately over rice.

minced_pork.hint: No pork? Finely chop beef sirloin, or skip the meat entirely for a vegetarian version.

wok.hint: A deep skillet works; stir more gently so the tofu cubes stay whole.

steps: Cut the tofu into 3/4-inch cubes and soak in hot salted water for 5 minutes. Drain well — this stops it breaking apart.
Brown the minced pork in 1 tbsp oil over high heat until the fat renders, about 2 minutes.
Add 1 tbsp doubanjiang and minced garlic. Fry 30 seconds until the oil turns red.
Add 3/4 cup water, bring to a simmer, and slide in the tofu. Simmer gently for 4 minutes.
Thicken with a cornstarch slurry (1 tsp cornstarch + 2 tsp water), stir once, and finish with ground Sichuan peppercorn and scallion.

frying_pan.hint: No skillet? Blanch in a pot and finish with a garlic-oil drizzle.

gas_stove.hint: An electric hob works; expect an extra minute to get things sizzling.

steps: Cut the broccoli into even florets and soak 5 minutes in cold water, then drain very well.
Heat 1 tbsp oil over medium-high, add sliced garlic, and fry for 20 seconds until fragrant but not brown.
Add the broccoli and stir-fry 2 minutes without water — the wok-dry heat is the point.
Splash in 2 tbsp water, cover for 90 seconds to steam the stems, then uncover and finish on high heat.
Season with salt and an optional drizzle of oyster sauce.

steamer_pot.hint: No steamer? Set a steaming rack inside a deep pot with 1 inch of simmering water, cover with a lid, and steam in a heatproof bowl.

steps: Beat 3 eggs with 1 1/2 cups warm water (not hot) and 1/2 tsp salt — the ratio is 1 part egg to 1.5 parts water.
Strain the mixture through a sieve into a shallow bowl and skim off the bubbles. This is the whole secret to a smooth custard.
Cover the bowl with a plate or foil. Steam over gently simmering water for 10 minutes — never a rolling boil.
Rest 2 minutes, then drizzle with light soy sauce and sesame oil. Serve warm.

clay_pot.hint: No clay pot? A heavy-bottomed stockpot with the lid on gives nearly the same result — just check the liquid every 20 minutes.

steps: Cut pork belly into 1-inch cubes. Blanch in boiling water for 3 minutes, then rinse and pat dry.
Caramelize 2 tbsp sugar in 1 tbsp oil over medium heat until amber, then add the pork and coat evenly.
Add ginger, star anise, 2 tbsp Shaoxing wine, 1 tbsp dark soy sauce, and hot water to cover.
Simmer covered for 60 minutes over the lowest heat until a chopstick slides through cleanly.
Uncover and reduce on high heat for 10 minutes until the sauce clings to each cube and turns glossy.
Slice the pork against the grain into thin matchsticks. Toss with 1 tbsp light soy sauce, 1 tsp cornstarch and a splash of water; rest 10 minutes.
Soak the wood ear in warm water 15 minutes, then shred. Julienne the carrot. Mix the sauce: 2 tbsp sugar, 2 tbsp black vinegar, 1 tbsp light soy sauce, 1 tbsp cornstarch, 4 tbsp water.
Stir-fry the pork in a hot oiled wok 90 seconds and remove. Fry doubanjiang, chopped pickled chili, garlic and ginger 30 seconds until the oil turns red, add the vegetables for 1 minute.
Return the pork, pour in the sauce and toss until glossy, about 40 seconds. Finish with scallion.
Simmer the whole slab of pork belly with ginger and shaoxing wine for 20 minutes, until a chopstick slides in with slight resistance. Cool, then slice as thin as you can.
Render the slices in a dry wok over medium heat until they curl at the edges and the fat turns translucent, about 4 minutes. Push them to one side.
Fry doubanjiang, douchi and sweet bean sauce in the rendered fat 40 seconds, then toss everything together with green pepper and garlic sprout over high heat for 2 minutes.
Slice the beef across the grain into thin sheets. Marinate 15 minutes in shaoxing wine, 1 tbsp light soy sauce, 1 tbsp cornstarch and 2 tbsp water.
Blanch the bean sprouts 1 minute and spread them in a deep serving bowl.
Fry doubanjiang, ginger and half the garlic in 2 tbsp oil until fragrant, add 700 ml water and simmer 5 minutes. Slide in the beef sheet by sheet and poach 90 seconds — do not stir hard.
Pour everything over the sprouts. Top with chili flakes, crushed Sichuan peppercorn and the rest of the garlic, then pour 4 tbsp smoking-hot oil over the top.
Slice the fish fillets into 1 cm pieces. Mix with salt, shaoxing wine and 2 tbsp cornstarch; rest 15 minutes. The starch coating is what keeps the fish whole.
Spread blanched bean sprouts in a deep bowl. Fry doubanjiang, ginger and garlic in oil until red, add 800 ml water and simmer 5 minutes.
Lower the fish in gently and poach 60–90 seconds, just until opaque. Pour over the sprouts, scatter chili flakes and crushed peppercorn, and splash with hot oil.
Poach the chicken thighs with ginger and shaoxing wine: bring to a bare simmer, cook 12 minutes, then turn off the heat and leave covered 8 minutes. Plunge into ice water — this tightens the skin.
Whisk 3 tbsp chili oil, 1 tbsp sesame paste, 2 tbsp light soy sauce, 1 tbsp black vinegar, 1 tsp sugar and 2 minced garlic cloves into a pourable sauce.
Chop the chicken into bite-size pieces, spoon the sauce over, and finish with crushed peanuts and scallion.
Cut the chicken into 2 cm cubes and marinate 20 minutes in shaoxing wine, light soy sauce, salt and 1 tbsp cornstarch.
Heat 3 cm of oil to 170°C and fry the chicken 3 minutes until pale gold. Raise the heat and fry again 60 seconds until crisp and deep golden. Drain.
In a dry wok, toast the dried chilies and peppercorn 30 seconds, add garlic and ginger, then return the chicken and toss 1 minute. The chilies should smell toasted, not burnt.
Trim the beans and dry them completely — water on the surface will spit in the oil. Fry in 1 cm of oil over medium-high heat 5 minutes until wrinkled and blistered. Drain.
Pour off most of the oil and brown the minced pork, breaking it up, about 2 minutes.
Add garlic, dried chili and chopped preserved mustard greens, fry 30 seconds, return the beans and season with light soy sauce and a pinch of sugar.
Simmer the pork belly with ginger and shaoxing wine for 25 minutes, until firm but yielding. Chill in ice water 10 minutes, then slice paper-thin — cold meat slices cleaner.
Mash 4 garlic cloves with a pinch of salt into a paste. Stir in 2 tbsp chili oil, 2 tbsp light soy sauce, 1 tsp sugar and 1 tsp black vinegar.
Arrange the slices over sliced cucumber, spoon the garlic sauce over, and let it sit 5 minutes before serving.
Soak the glass noodles in warm water 10 minutes until pliable, then drain and cut into 10 cm lengths.
Brown the minced pork in a hot wok, then add doubanjiang, garlic and ginger and fry 40 seconds until the oil reddens.
Add 200 ml water and the noodles, toss over medium heat 2 minutes until the noodles absorb the liquid and turn glossy. Finish with scallion.
Fry the minced pork hard until crisp, then stir in 1 tsp doubanjiang and 1 tsp sweet bean sauce with a splash of soy. This is the dry-fried topping.
For each bowl: 1 tbsp sesame paste, 1 tbsp chili oil, 1 tbsp light soy sauce, 1 tsp black vinegar, 1 minced garlic clove, a pinch of sugar and 2 tbsp hot water. Whisk smooth.
Boil the noodles, lift straight into the bowls with a little cooking water, then top with the pork, crushed peppercorn, preserved greens and scallion. Toss before eating.

Soak the glass noodles in warm water 10 minutes. Meanwhile build the bowl: 2 tbsp black vinegar, 1 tbsp chili oil, 1 tbsp light soy sauce, 1 tsp sugar, 1 minced garlic clove and a pinch of ground pepper.
Bring 500 ml water or stock to a rolling boil, add the bean sprouts for 30 seconds, then the noodles for 60–90 seconds — they should be slippery but still springy.
Ladle noodles and broth into the bowl, stir once, and top with crushed peanuts and scallion.
Mix the pork with grated ginger, chopped scallion, 1 tbsp light soy sauce, 1 tsp cornstarch and 2 tbsp water, stirring in one direction until sticky.
Put a teaspoon of filling in each wrapper, fold in half and pinch the corners together. Keep the wrappers covered so they do not dry out.

Boil 2 minutes until they float and the skins wrinkle. Bowl: 1 tbsp chili oil, 1 tbsp light soy sauce, 1 tsp black vinegar, 1 tsp sugar, minced garlic. Lift the wontons in with a splash of cooking water.
Cut the eggplant into fat batons, salt them 10 minutes and squeeze out the water. Shallow-fry 4 minutes until collapsed and golden, then drain.
Brown the pork, add doubanjiang, chopped pickled chili, garlic and ginger, and fry until the oil is red.
Mix 2 tbsp sugar, 2 tbsp black vinegar, 1 tbsp light soy sauce, 1 tbsp cornstarch and 5 tbsp water; pour in with the eggplant and simmer 2 minutes until the sauce clings.

Butterfly the shrimp, pat dry, and toss with salt, 1 tsp cornstarch and a splash of shaoxing wine. Mix the sauce: 1 tbsp sugar, 1 tbsp black vinegar, 1 tbsp light soy sauce, 1 tsp cornstarch, 3 tbsp water.
Fry dried chilies and peppercorn in hot oil 20 seconds, add garlic, ginger and the white parts of the scallion, then the shrimp. Cook 90 seconds until they curl and turn pink.
Pour in the sauce and toss until it glazes the shrimp, then fold in the peanuts off the heat so they stay crunchy.
Boil the noodles 1 minute short of the package time, drain, rinse under cold water and toss with a teaspoon of sesame oil so they do not clump.
Whisk 1 tbsp sesame paste, 1 tbsp chili oil, 2 tbsp light soy sauce, 1 tbsp black vinegar, 2 tsp sugar, 1 minced garlic clove and 2 tbsp cold water.
Toss the noodles with julienned cucumber and the sauce, then scatter crushed peanuts and scallion.

dishes.nameEn: Braised Fish in Chili Bean Paste
steps: Score the fish twice on each side, rub with salt and shaoxing wine, and pat dry. Sear in a hot oiled wok 3 minutes per side until the skin releases cleanly. Set aside.
Fry doubanjiang, ginger and garlic in the same pan 40 seconds, add 300 ml water, 1 tbsp soy sauce and 1 tsp sugar, then slide the fish back in.
Braise 8 minutes, spooning sauce over the fish. Lift it out, thicken the sauce with cornstarch slurry, add a few drops of vinegar and pour over. Finish with scallion.
Tear the cabbage into palm-size pieces with your hands — the ragged edges catch sauce better than a knife cut. Discard the thick core.
Get a wok smoking hot with 2 tbsp oil, add dried chilies and garlic and stir 10 seconds.
Add the cabbage and stir-fry 90 seconds over the highest heat. Splash vinegar down the side of the wok, season with soy and a pinch of sugar, and serve while still crisp.
Trim the claws and split each foot in half lengthwise so the brine reaches the bone. Poach 10 minutes with ginger and shaoxing wine.
Chill in ice water 10 minutes; this is what makes the skin springy rather than soft.
Mix 200 ml cold water with 4 tbsp rice vinegar, 2 tbsp sugar, 1 tbsp salt, chopped pickled chilies and dried chilies. Submerge the feet and refrigerate at least 4 hours, ideally overnight.
Slice the pork thinly, then massage in 1 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp cornstarch and 2 tbsp water. Rest 15 minutes.
Blanch the sprouts and spread in a bowl. Fry doubanjiang, ginger and garlic in oil, add 600 ml water and simmer 5 minutes.
Slide the pork in and poach 90 seconds. Pour over the sprouts, top with chili flakes, crushed peppercorn and garlic, and pour hot oil over the top.
Pat the tofu dry and cut into 2 cm cubes. Pan-fry in a little oil until all sides are golden and crisp, about 6 minutes. Drain on paper.
Mix 1 tbsp sugar, 1 tbsp black vinegar, 1 tbsp light soy sauce, 1 tsp cornstarch and 3 tbsp water.
Fry chilies, peppercorn, garlic and scallion whites 30 seconds, return the tofu, pour in the sauce and toss gently. Add peanuts last.
Halve the melon, scrape out the seeds and white pith — that pith is where most of the bitterness lives. Slice thin, salt 10 minutes, then squeeze dry.
Dry-fry the slices in a hot wok without oil for 3 minutes until the edges brown and the bitterness mellows.
Add 1 tbsp oil, garlic, dried chili and douchi, fry 30 seconds, then season with soy and a pinch of sugar.
Split the green peppers with your thumb and tear into rough pieces. Dry-fry them in a hot wok 2 minutes until blistered and softened, then set aside.
Slice the pork belly thin and fry in its own fat until the edges brown, about 3 minutes.
Add garlic and douchi, fry 20 seconds, return the peppers, splash shaoxing wine and season with light soy sauce. Toss 1 minute over the highest heat.
Slice the beef across the grain as thin as possible. Toss with soy sauce, 1 tsp cornstarch and 1 tbsp oil; rest 10 minutes.
Heat the wok until it smokes, add 2 tbsp oil and the beef. Spread it flat, sear 30 seconds, toss 20 seconds and remove — it should still be pink inside.
Fry green pepper, dried chili, garlic and ginger 40 seconds, return the beef, splash shaoxing wine and toss 20 seconds. Serve immediately.
Cut the pork into 3 cm cubes and blanch 3 minutes in boiling water. Drain and dry.
Caramelize 2 tbsp sugar in 1 tbsp oil until deep amber, then add the pork and turn to coat. Add ginger, scallion, star anise and dried chilies.

Pour in shaoxing wine and enough hot water to cover, plus 1 tbsp dark and 2 tbsp light soy sauce. Braise in a clay pot, barely simmering, 50 minutes, then reduce uncovered 10 minutes until the sauce coats the meat.
Score the fish, rub inside and out with shaoxing wine and a pinch of salt, and lay ginger slices in the cavity and under the fish.
Mix 4 tbsp chopped chili with minced garlic and 1 tsp oil. Spread over the fish, then steam over rapidly boiling water 8–10 minutes for a 500 g fish.
Pour off the cloudy liquid in the plate, drizzle with light soy sauce, top with scallion, and pour 2 tbsp hot oil over to release the aroma.
Char the whole green peppers directly in a dry wok over high heat 6 minutes, turning, until the skin blackens in patches and the flesh softens. Cover 5 minutes, then peel off the loose skin.
Tear the peppers into strips and put them in a mortar with 2 garlic cloves and a pinch of salt.
Pound roughly — you want texture, not paste. Add quartered century egg, 1 tbsp black vinegar, 1 tsp soy sauce and a drizzle of sesame oil, and fold together.
Beat 4 eggs with a pinch of salt until no streaks remain.
Fry the chopped chili with 1 tsp oil in a hot pan 30 seconds to drive off the raw edge, then push to one side.
Add the eggs and scramble over medium heat, folding slowly, until just set. Stir in the chili and finish with scallion.
Chop the duck into pieces and blanch 5 minutes to remove the gamey edge. Drain well and pat dry.
Fry ginger, garlic, star anise and dried chilies in oil, add the duck and render 5 minutes until the skin browns.
Add shaoxing wine, 1 tbsp dark soy, 2 tbsp light soy, 1 tbsp sugar and hot water to cover. Simmer covered 35 minutes, then reduce 10 minutes until glossy.
Rinse the sausage and slice on a deep diagonal about 5 mm thick — more surface means more caramelized fat.
Arrange in a shallow dish with a few shreds of ginger and a teaspoon of shaoxing wine.
Steam over boiling water 12 minutes. Serve with the rendered fat spooned back over.
Slice the potatoes 5 mm thick, soak 5 minutes in water and dry thoroughly. Pan-fry in a little oil 4 minutes per side until golden and cooked through.
Fry the sliced pork belly until the fat renders, then add doubanjiang, garlic and dried chilies and fry 40 seconds.
Return the potatoes with the green pepper and soy sauce, toss 2 minutes over high heat until every slice is coated red.
Fry the pork until crisp with a splash of soy sauce. Set aside as the topping.
Build the bowl: 1 tbsp chili oil, 1 tbsp light soy sauce, 1 tsp black vinegar, 1 tsp sugar, 1 minced garlic clove, a pinch of ground peppercorn and 2 tbsp hot noodle water.
Boil the noodles and a handful of greens, lift into the bowl, and top with the pork, crushed peanuts and scallion.
Mix the pork with grated ginger, 1 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tsp cornstarch and 3 tbsp water, stirring until it holds together.
Fill and seal the wrappers. Boil 3 minutes, adding a splash of cold water when the water threatens to boil over, until the wrappers turn translucent.
Sweet soy: simmer 3 tbsp soy sauce with 2 tbsp sugar for 2 minutes. Spoon over the dumplings with chili oil and plenty of mashed garlic.
Simmer 3 tbsp soy sauce and 3 tbsp sugar with 2 tbsp water for 3 minutes until syrupy. Let cool.
Boil thick noodles until just tender, 1 minute past al dente, then drain and toss with a little oil.
Toss with the sweet soy, 1 tbsp chili oil, 1 tsp sesame paste and minced garlic. Top with crushed peanuts.
Bring a pot of water with ginger and scallion to 90°C — small bubbles, not a rolling boil. Lower the chicken in, cover, and hold at that temperature 18 minutes for thighs.
Lift the chicken straight into ice water for 10 minutes. The sudden chill is what gives the skin its snap.
Chop into pieces. Make the dipping sauce: finely minced ginger and scallion, salted, then flooded with oil heated until it just smokes.
Simmer 250 ml light soy, 3 tbsp dark soy, 3 tbsp sugar, ginger, scallion and star anise with 400 ml water for 10 minutes to build the master poaching liquid.
Slide in the chicken thighs, bring back to a bare simmer and cook 18 minutes, turning once.
Turn off the heat and leave the chicken in the liquid 15 minutes to absorb color. Brush with a little of the braising liquid before chopping.
Cut the pork into long 4 cm-thick strips. Marinate overnight in 2 tbsp oyster sauce, 1 tbsp each light and dark soy, 2 tbsp sugar, 1 cube mashed fermented tofu, 1 tsp five spice and minced garlic.
Roast at 200°C for 20 minutes on a rack over a tray of water, turning once.
Brush with honey thinned with a spoon of the marinade and blast at 230°C for 5 minutes until the edges char. Rest 10 minutes before slicing.
Ask the butcher to cut the ribs into 2 cm pieces. Soak in cold water 20 minutes to pull out the blood, then dry thoroughly.
Marinate 20 minutes with 2 tbsp chopped douchi, minced garlic, 1 tbsp soy, 1 tsp sugar, 1 tbsp cornstarch and 1 tbsp oil — the starch keeps them tender.
Spread in a single layer in a shallow dish and steam over furious heat 12 minutes. Do not open the lid early.
Have the fish cleaned and scored. Rub with a little salt and shaoxing wine, stuff the cavity with ginger and lay it on a plate over two chopsticks so steam circulates.
Steam over rolling boil 8 minutes for a 500 g fish. Test at the bone — it should flake but still look moist.
Pour off the cloudy liquid, replace the ginger with fresh scallion. Drizzle 2 tbsp light soy sauce mixed with a pinch of sugar, then pour 2 tbsp smoking oil over the scallion.
Soak the glass noodles 10 minutes, drain, and spread over the bottom of a shallow dish.
Butterfly the shrimp along the back, flatten them, and lay on the noodles. Fry half the minced garlic in oil until golden, mix with the raw garlic and 1 tbsp soy sauce, and spoon over.
Steam 6 minutes, then scatter scallion and pour a spoon of hot oil over the top.
Blanch the bok choy in boiling salted water 60 seconds, stems first, then plunge into cold water to keep the green.
Warm 1 tbsp oil, fry garlic 20 seconds, add 2 tbsp oyster sauce, 1 tsp sugar and 4 tbsp water.
Thicken with a teaspoon of cornstarch slurry, pour over the drained greens and finish with sesame oil.
Trim the thick stems and peel any stringy skin. Drop into boiling water with a slice of ginger and 1 tsp oil — the oil keeps the surface glossy.
Cook 90 seconds, until the stem yields to a knife but still snaps. Drain standing up so the water runs off.
Lay on a plate, pour over 2 tbsp oyster sauce loosened with a spoon of hot water, and top with garlic fried in oil until just golden.
Rinse 1.5 cups rice and soak 30 minutes. Drain, put in the clay pot with 1.4 cups water and 1 tsp oil, and bring to a boil.
When the water disappears and small craters form, lay sliced sausage on top, cover, and cook on the lowest heat 12 minutes. Rotate the pot every 3 minutes so the crust forms evenly.
Rest off heat 5 minutes. Drizzle with 2 tbsp light soy, 1 tsp dark soy and 1 tsp sugar warmed together, and scatter scallion.
Pat the shrimp dry, toss with salt, white pepper and 1 tsp cornstarch. Sear 45 seconds per side and remove.
Beat 4 eggs with 1 tbsp water and 1 tsp cornstarch slurry — the starch is what makes them silky rather than rubbery.
Lower the heat to medium-low, add the eggs and stir slowly with a spatula, pulling the set curds to the center. When 70% set, fold in the shrimp and take off the heat.
Cut the pork into 2 cm cubes, marinate 15 minutes with soy sauce, salt and a beaten egg, then coat heavily in cornstarch.
Fry at 165°C for 3 minutes, rest 5 minutes, then fry again at 190°C for 90 seconds. Double frying is what keeps the crust crisp under sauce.
Stir-fry garlic and bell pepper 1 minute, add 3 tbsp sugar, 3 tbsp vinegar, 1 tbsp soy and 4 tbsp water, thicken, then fold in the pork off the heat.
Rub the chicken inside and out with shaoxing wine and a pinch of white pepper, then wrap in parchment with ginger and scallion.
Spread a 2 cm bed of coarse salt in a baking tray, bury the parcel, and bake at 200°C for 45 minutes.
Crack the salt crust, unwrap, and brush the skin with sesame oil. Rest 10 minutes, then chop. The meat should be barely seasoned by the salt — that is the point.
Slide the silken tofu out of its box onto a plate and cut into 8 blocks with a wet knife.
Quarter the century egg and tuck the pieces between the tofu blocks.
Spoon over 1 tbsp light soy sauce, 1 tsp sesame oil and a few drops of chili oil. Scatter scallion and serve cold.
Blend half the corn kernels with 600 ml water until smooth; keep the rest whole for texture.
Simmer both corns with a pinch of salt 8 minutes, then thicken with 2 tbsp cornstarch slurry until it coats a spoon.
Stream in a beaten egg while stirring slowly in one direction, then stop immediately — over-stirring shreds the ribbons.
Chop the chicken into 3 cm pieces. Marinate 20 minutes with sliced shiitake, ginger, 1 tbsp oyster sauce, 1 tbsp soy, 1 tbsp cornstarch and a splash of shaoxing wine.
Spread in a shallow dish in one layer — piled up, the middle will not cook through.
Steam over high heat 15 minutes. Finish with scallion and a few drops of sesame oil.
Boil the noodles 1 minute short, drain, rinse cold and toss with a little oil. Spread out to dry 10 minutes.
Mix 2 tbsp light soy, 1 tsp dark soy and 1 tsp sugar.
Get the wok very hot, add oil and noodles, press flat 30 seconds to crisp, then toss with bean sprouts and scallion. Pour the sauce around the rim of the wok and toss 1 minute.
Blanch the ribs 3 minutes in boiling water with ginger, then drain and dry.
Fry the ribs in 2 tbsp oil until browned on all sides, about 5 minutes.
Add 3 tbsp sugar, 3 tbsp black vinegar, 1 tbsp soy, 1 tbsp shaoxing wine and 200 ml water. Simmer covered 30 minutes, then reduce uncovered until the sauce is sticky and clings.
Soak the wood ear 15 minutes, chop finely, and mix with the pork, grated ginger, 1 tbsp soy, 1 tbsp cornstarch and 2 tbsp water.
Stir in one direction for 2 minutes until the mixture turns sticky — this is what gives the patty its bounce.
Press into a 2 cm-thick disc in a shallow dish and steam 12 minutes. Pour off the juice, or spoon it back over.
Rinse 1 cup rice and rub it with 1 tsp oil and a pinch of salt. Freeze 30 minutes if you have time — broken grains release starch faster.
Simmer the rice in 2 litres water with sliced ginger for 40 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes, until the grains break down.
Marinate the pork with salt, white pepper and a splash of water. Add with diced century egg and cook 5 minutes. Season and top with scallion.
Keep the shells on — they crisp and hold the seasoning. Slit the back, devein, and pat very dry.
Toss with cornstarch and fry at 190°C for 90 seconds until the shells turn translucent and crisp. Drain.
Fry garlic, chili and scallion 20 seconds, return the shrimp, and toss with a mix of 1 tsp salt and 2 tsp black pepper.
Cut the brisket into 4 cm chunks and blanch 5 minutes. Drain and rinse off the scum.
Fry ginger, star anise and 1 tsp doubanjiang in oil, add the beef and brown, then splash shaoxing wine with 1 tbsp dark and 2 tbsp light soy and 1 tbsp sugar.
Cover with hot water and simmer 70 minutes. Add daikon chunks and cook 25 minutes more, until a chopstick passes through the beef with no resistance.
Cut the silken tofu into thick slabs and lay in a shallow dish. Pat the shrimp dry and curl one on top of each slab.
Steam 6 minutes over boiling water — the tofu should quiver, not collapse.
Pour off the water, drizzle 1 tbsp light soy mixed with a teaspoon of oyster sauce, and finish with scallion and hot oil.
Peel the winter melon, remove the seed core, and cut into 1 cm slices. Blanch 2 minutes to set them.
Marinate the shrimp with salt, white pepper and 1 tsp cornstarch, then sear 1 minute and remove.
Fry garlic and ginger, add the melon with 100 ml water and simmer 4 minutes until translucent, return the shrimp and thicken lightly.
Chop the chicken into pieces and marinate 20 minutes with oyster sauce, both soys, sugar and cornstarch.
Heat the clay pot until smoking, add oil, then a thick layer of ginger, garlic and scallion whites. Fry 1 minute until fragrant.
Lay the chicken on top, cover, and cook over medium heat 12 minutes without opening. Splash shaoxing wine around the lid at the table for the sizzle.
Separate the rice noodles by hand while cold. If they are refrigerated, microwave 40 seconds to soften — torn noodles mean a broken dish.
Marinate the beef with soy, cornstarch and oil, then sear in a smoking wok 45 seconds and remove.
Add oil, the noodles, and press them flat 20 seconds before tossing. Add soy sauces, return the beef with sprouts and scallion, and toss 40 seconds — no more.
Bring 2 litres water to a boil with thick ginger slices and scallion. Keep the shrimp whole and cold until the last second.
Drop them in and cook 100 seconds, until they curl into a C and the shells turn coral. A tight O means overcooked.
Serve with a dip of light soy, minced garlic, a few drops of sesame oil and chili oil to taste.
Slice the beef thin across the grain. Marinate 15 minutes with 1 tbsp soy, 1 tbsp cornstarch, 1 tbsp water and 1 tsp oil.
Sear in a very hot wok 45 seconds, then remove while still pink.
Fry garlic 15 seconds, add 2 tbsp oyster sauce, 1 tsp sugar and 3 tbsp water, return the beef and toss 30 seconds. Finish with scallion.
Split the shrimp along the back and pat dry. Dust lightly with cornstarch so the sauce grabs.
Fry in a hot wok 90 seconds per side until the shells blister, then remove.
Add more oil, a lot of julienned ginger and scallion, fry 40 seconds, return the shrimp and splash shaoxing wine and soy sauce.
Cut the pork belly into 1 cm dice. Render in a dry pot 6 minutes until the fat runs and the edges brown.
Add sliced garlic, ginger, 3 tbsp light soy, 1 tbsp dark soy, 2 tbsp sugar, 1 tsp five spice and a splash of shaoxing wine. Stir 1 minute.
Add 400 ml water and simmer 45 minutes until the sauce is thick and glossy. Serve over hot rice with a halved boiled egg if you like.
Chop the chicken into pieces and pat dry. Slice ginger into coins and smash the garlic cloves.
Heat 3 tbsp sesame oil gently and fry the ginger 4 minutes until it curls at the edges — do not let it brown, or it turns bitter.
Add garlic and chicken, brown 5 minutes, then pour in 3 tbsp soy, 3 tbsp shaoxing wine and 1 tbsp sugar. Cover and cook 12 minutes, then reduce until sticky.
Cut the chicken into bite-size pieces and marinate 30 minutes with soy sauce, garlic, 1 tsp five spice and white pepper.
Coat each piece in cornstarch, press it on, then shake off the excess. Rest 5 minutes so the coating hydrates.
Fry at 170°C for 3 minutes, then at 190°C for 60 seconds. Toss the hot chicken with salt, white pepper and a pinch of five spice.
Fry thick ginger slices in 4 tbsp sesame oil over low heat 5 minutes until fragrant and just beginning to crisp.
Add the chicken pieces and brown 5 minutes on all sides.
Pour in 200 ml shaoxing wine and 200 ml water, simmer covered 25 minutes. Season with salt only — the wine and sesame carry the dish.
Soak the rice noodles in warm water 15 minutes until flexible, then cut into shorter lengths with scissors.
Fry dried shrimp, garlic and pork until fragrant, add shredded cabbage and shiitake and cook 3 minutes until softened.
Add 200 ml water, 2 tbsp soy and a splash of oyster sauce, then the noodles. Toss with chopsticks 3 minutes until the liquid is absorbed.
Boil the eggs 8 minutes, cool, and crack the shells lightly all over so the braise seeps in. Cut the dried tofu into thick slices.
Simmer 300 ml water with 3 tbsp light soy, 1 tbsp dark soy, 2 tbsp sugar, star anise, garlic and 1 tsp five spice for 10 minutes.
Add the eggs and tofu and simmer gently 25 minutes. Better after sitting in the liquid overnight.
Cut firm tofu into 4 cm squares and hollow out a shallow pocket in the center with a small spoon.
Mix the pork with chopped dried shrimp, scallion, 1 tbsp soy, 1 tsp cornstarch and a pinch of white pepper. Press a spoonful into each pocket and dust the surface with cornstarch.
Fry filling-side down first, 3 minutes, until golden and sealed. Flip, add 150 ml water and 1 tbsp oyster sauce, cover and simmer 8 minutes.

dishes.nameEn: Pork Belly with Preserved Mustard Greens
steps: Boil the pork slab 25 minutes, drain, and rub the skin with dark soy. Fry skin-side down in a little oil until blistered — stand back, it spits.
Soak the preserved greens 20 minutes, rinse, squeeze, and fry with garlic, 1 tbsp soy and 1 tsp sugar for 3 minutes.
Slice the pork 1 cm thick, lay skin-down in a bowl, pack the greens on top with the braising liquid, and steam 60 minutes. Invert onto a plate.
Use a lot of old ginger — 100 g — sliced thick. Fry it in 3 tbsp sesame oil over low heat 6 minutes until dry and fragrant.
Add duck pieces and brown 8 minutes, rendering the skin.
Pour in 300 ml shaoxing wine and 400 ml water, add 2 tbsp soy and 1 tbsp sugar, and simmer covered 60 minutes until the meat pulls from the bone.
Use cold day-old rice and break up any clumps with wet hands.
Dice the sausage and render it in a dry pan 3 minutes until the fat turns the pan red. Push aside, scramble the eggs in the fat.
Add the rice, press flat 30 seconds, then toss with soy sauce and white pepper. Finish with scallion.
Whisk 100 g flour, 200 ml water and a pinch of salt into a thin batter. Rest 10 minutes.
Pour a thin layer into a lightly oiled non-stick pan over medium heat, cook 90 seconds until the edges lift.
Crack an egg on top, spread it over the crepe with a pinch of salt and scallion, flip for 30 seconds, roll up and cut into segments.
Cut the cabbage into 3 cm squares, separating the thick stems from the leaves.
Fry garlic in hot oil 15 seconds, add the stems first for 1 minute, then the leaves.
Splash 1 tbsp soy and 1 tbsp water, cover 90 seconds, then finish with 2 tbsp oyster sauce off the heat.
Slice the pork into 3 mm sheets, pound them thin, and marinate 10 minutes with salt and a splash of shaoxing wine.
Make a thick batter with 100 g cornstarch, water and a little oil. Coat each slice and fry at 170°C for 90 seconds, then at 200°C for 40 seconds until blistered.
Stir-fry carrot and scallion 30 seconds, add 3 tbsp sugar, 3 tbsp rice vinegar and 1 tbsp soy, bring to a boil, then toss the pork in the sauce for 10 seconds only — it must stay crisp.
Cut the pork into thin shreds and marinate 15 minutes with soy sauce, shaoxing wine, 1 tsp cornstarch and a little water.
Fry the pork in a hot wok 90 seconds until just cooked, then push aside.
Fry 3 tbsp sweet bean sauce with 1 tbsp sugar and 2 tbsp water for 40 seconds until glossy, toss with the pork, and serve over a bed of shredded scallion.
Soak the wood ear 15 minutes and shred. Slice the pork thin and marinate 10 minutes with soy and cornstarch. Julienne the cucumber.
Scramble 2 eggs in a hot wok, break into pieces and remove while still soft.
Fry the pork 1 minute, add wood ear and cucumber 1 minute, return the eggs, season with soy and a splash of shaoxing wine, finish with scallion.
Slice the lamb across the grain as thin as possible. Marinate 10 minutes with shaoxing wine, soy sauce and 1 tsp oil.
Cut the scallion into 4 cm lengths, keeping the white and green parts separate.
Smoke the wok, add oil and the lamb, spread flat 20 seconds, then toss. Add scallion whites and garlic, toss 30 seconds, then the greens, and splash vinegar down the side.
Slice the lamb thin and toss with soy sauce, 1 tsp cornstarch and 1 tbsp oil. Rest 15 minutes.
Dry-toast the cumin seeds 40 seconds until they smell nutty, then crush lightly.
Sear the lamb in a smoking wok 90 seconds, add onion and garlic for 1 minute, then toss with the cumin, chili flakes and salt off the heat so the spices do not burn.
Mix 500 g pork with 1 egg, 3 tbsp cornstarch, grated ginger, scallion, 1 tbsp soy and 3 tbsp water. Stir in one direction 3 minutes, then slap the mixture against the bowl 10 times.
Shape into four large balls and fry in 170°C oil, turning, until evenly browned, about 5 minutes.
Braise with 2 tbsp soy, 1 tsp dark soy, 1 tbsp sugar, star anise and water to half-cover, 40 minutes. Thicken the sauce and pour over.
Separate the cabbage leaves and cut the thick stems into bite-size pieces, keeping them apart from the leaves.
Fry dried chilies and garlic in hot oil 15 seconds, add the stems and stir-fry 2 minutes.
Add the leaves, splash 2 tbsp black vinegar and 1 tbsp soy mixed with 1 tsp sugar, toss 1 minute, then thicken with a light cornstarch slurry.
Cut potato, eggplant and green pepper into irregular chunks of similar size. Soak the potato 5 minutes and dry it.
Shallow-fry the potato 4 minutes, then the eggplant 4 minutes until collapsed and golden. Drain both.
Fry garlic 20 seconds, add 2 tbsp soy, 1 tsp sugar, 1 tsp vinegar and 5 tbsp water, thicken, then fold in all three vegetables and toss 30 seconds.
Peel the sweet potato and cut into 3 cm chunks. Dust with flour and fry at 170°C for 5 minutes until a skewer slides in easily.
Drain the oil and wipe the wok. Melt 4 tbsp sugar with 1 tbsp oil over low heat, swirling, until it turns pale amber — about 90 seconds.
Kill the heat, add the sweet potato and fold fast until each piece is lacquered. Serve immediately with a bowl of cold water for dipping.
Fry 300 g minced pork in 3 tbsp oil until dry and crumbly, about 5 minutes.
Add 5 tbsp sweet bean sauce, ginger and scallion, then 150 ml water. Simmer 15 minutes, stirring, until the oil separates and floats — that is a proper zha jiang.
Boil the noodles, rinse briefly, and top with the sauce and julienned cucumber.
Chop the cabbage fine, salt it 15 minutes, then squeeze out as much water as you can — wet filling tears wrappers.
Mix the pork with ginger, scallion, 2 tbsp soy, 1 tbsp sesame oil and the cabbage. Stir in one direction until sticky.
Fill and pleat the wrappers. Boil in batches, adding a cup of cold water each time it boils, for 6 minutes total. Serve with vinegar and garlic.
Scramble 4 eggs in oil until just set, then chop fine and cool completely.
Chop the chives and toss them with 2 tbsp sesame oil before adding anything salty — the oil coats the cut edges and stops them weeping.
Fold in the egg, salt and a pinch of white pepper. Fill, seal, and boil 5 minutes.
Make a soft dough with 300 g flour and 180 ml hot water. Knead 5 minutes, cover, rest 30 minutes.
Scramble and chop the eggs, chop the chives, and mix with oil, salt and white pepper just before filling.
Roll the dough into thin rounds, add filling to one half, fold and pinch the edge. Pan-fry 3 minutes per side over medium-low until spotted.
Mix 300 g flour with 180 ml hot water into a shaggy dough, knead smooth, and rest 30 minutes.
Roll thin, brush with oil, scatter salt and chopped scallion, then roll up like a cigar and coil into a spiral. Flatten gently.
Pan-fry in 2 tbsp oil over medium heat 3 minutes per side, pressing with the spatula, until deep golden and flaky.
Whisk 100 g flour with 200 ml water and a pinch of salt until completely smooth. Rest 10 minutes.
Pour a thin layer into a hot oiled pan and swirl to cover. Cook 60 seconds until the underside sets.
Crack an egg over the top, spread it with the back of a spoon, scatter scallion, and flip for 40 seconds. Roll and cut.
Cut the pork belly into thick 2 cm slices and blanch 3 minutes.
Tie each slice with twine if you want it to hold shape. Lay them in a pot with ginger, scallion, star anise, 4 tbsp light soy, 1 tbsp dark soy, 2 tbsp sugar and shaoxing wine.
Add water to cover and simmer very gently 80 minutes. The meat should wobble but not fall apart. Serve over rice with the braising liquid.
Score the fish in a deep diamond pattern on both sides, rub with salt and shaoxing wine, then coat every cut with dry cornstarch.
Hold the fish by the tail and ladle 180°C oil over it to set the shape, then lower it in and fry 4 minutes per side until crisp.
Fry ginger and garlic, add 4 tbsp sugar, 4 tbsp black vinegar, 2 tbsp soy and 100 ml water, thicken, and pour over the fish at the table.
Slice the liver 5 mm thick, rinse in cold water until it stops bleeding, then marinate 10 minutes with shaoxing wine, soy and cornstarch.
Blanch in boiling water 20 seconds and drain — this removes the metallic edge and stops it turning grainy.
Stir-fry garlic and ginger, add wood ear and cucumber 1 minute, return the liver, splash the sauce and toss 30 seconds only.
Soak the wood ear 15 minutes, then shred it and the tofu into thin strips.
Simmer 800 ml stock with the wood ear, tofu and dried shrimp 5 minutes. Season with 2 tbsp soy and 1 tsp salt.
Thicken with 3 tbsp cornstarch slurry, stream in a beaten egg, then add 3 tbsp black vinegar and 1 tsp white pepper off the heat — boiling after the vinegar kills its sharpness.
Bring 700 ml water or light stock to a boil with a pinch of salt.
Thicken with 1 tbsp cornstarch slurry so the egg can hang in ribbons instead of sinking.
Lower the heat, stream in 2 beaten eggs while stirring slowly once around the pot, then stop. Finish with sesame oil and scallion.
Cut the tomatoes into wedges. Fry them in 1 tbsp oil 4 minutes, pressing, until they collapse into a rough sauce.
Add 700 ml water and simmer 5 minutes with a pinch of sugar to balance the acidity.
Season, then stream in 2 beaten eggs and turn off the heat. Finish with sesame oil and scallion.
Soak the wood ear 15 minutes and shred. Slice the pork thin and the shiitake.
Fry scallion and pork 2 minutes, add wood ear and shiitake, then 700 ml stock and 2 tbsp soy. Simmer 10 minutes.
Thicken heavily with cornstarch slurry until it coats a spoon, stream in a beaten egg, and pour over freshly boiled noodles.
Soak the lamb chunks in cold water 30 minutes to draw out blood, then blanch 5 minutes and rinse.
Simmer with thick ginger slices and scallion in 2 litres water for 80 minutes, skimming the surface. Do not let it boil hard or the broth turns cloudy.
Season with salt and plenty of white pepper at the end. Serve with cilantro and chili oil.
Cut the brisket into 4 cm chunks and blanch 5 minutes, then rinse off the scum.
Simmer with ginger, star anise, 3 tbsp light soy and 1 tbsp dark soy in 2 litres water for 90 minutes, until the meat pulls apart with a fork.
Add daikon for the last 25 minutes. Cook the noodles separately, ladle the broth over, and finish with scallion and chili oil.
Salt the chopped cabbage 15 minutes and squeeze dry. Mix with pork, ginger, scallion and soy.
Fill the wrappers and pinch only the top seam, leaving the ends open — that shape sits flat and crisps better.
Fry in oil 2 minutes until the bases brown, add 100 ml water, cover, and steam 6 minutes. Uncover and let the water cook off until the bottoms crackle.
Dissolve 1 tsp yeast and 1 tbsp sugar in 260 ml warm water, add 500 g flour, knead 10 minutes, and rise covered until doubled, about 60 minutes.
Salt and squeeze the cabbage, mix with pork, ginger, scallion, soy and sesame oil. Chill so the filling is firm.
Punch down the dough, divide into 12, roll the edges thin and the center thick, fill and pleat. Rest 20 minutes, then steam 15 minutes and leave the lid on 3 minutes.
Mix 500 g flour, 1 tsp yeast, 1 tbsp sugar and 280 ml warm water. Knead 10 minutes and rise 60 minutes.
Roll into a large rectangle, brush with oil, scatter salt and scallion, roll up, and cut into 6 cm lengths. Twist each piece and pinch the ends under.
Rest 20 minutes, then steam 12 minutes over cold water brought to a boil. Do not lift the lid early.
Mix 500 g flour, 1 tsp yeast, 1 tbsp sugar and 270 ml warm water into a smooth dough. Knead 10 minutes until the surface is satin.
Divide into 8, shape into tall rounds, and rest 25 minutes until they spring back slowly when pressed.
Steam 15 minutes from cold water, then leave covered 5 minutes so they do not collapse.
Chop the chicken into 4 cm pieces. Fry sugar in oil until amber, add the chicken and brown deeply.
Add doubanjiang, ginger, garlic, star anise and dried chilies, fry 1 minute, then soy sauce and enough water to cover. Simmer 30 minutes.
Add potato chunks for 15 minutes, then green pepper for 5. Serve with wide noodles cooked separately and stirred through the sauce.
Cut the lamb into 2 cm cubes, leaving some fat on. Marinate 30 minutes with grated onion, salt, cumin and oil.
Thread onto skewers alternating lean and fat. Broil at 240°C for 12 minutes, turning once.
Sprinkle more cumin, chili flakes and salt in the last 2 minutes — adding spices at the start just burns them.
Cut lamb shoulder into large chunks with the bone in if possible. Soak in cold water 1 hour.
Cover with cold water, add ginger and onion, bring to a boil and skim carefully. Simmer 60 minutes — no spices, the meat should taste of itself.
Salt the cooking water only in the last 10 minutes, so the meat stays tender. Serve with raw onion and chili oil.
Simmer lamb with ginger 70 minutes, then shred the meat and keep the broth hot.
Make a stiff dough with flour and water, roll into thin rounds, and dry-fry in a pan until spotted. Tear into small pieces by hand.
Put the torn bread in a bowl with glass noodles, wood ear and lamb, ladle boiling broth over, and season with white pepper, cilantro and chili oil.
Braise the pork belly with soy sauces, sugar, star anise, ginger and five spice in water to cover for 90 minutes, until it shreds with a spoon.
Make a firm dough with 400 g flour, 1 tsp yeast and 200 ml water. Rest 40 minutes, then roll into flat rounds and pan-fry or bake until crisp outside.
Chop the pork with a little green pepper and cilantro, moisten with braising liquid, and stuff into split buns.
Boil wide noodles until just tender, 1 minute past al dente. Lift into a bowl with a handful of blanched greens.
Pile 1 tbsp chili flakes, minced garlic and scallion in the center of the noodles. Add 1 tbsp soy and 1 tbsp black vinegar around the edge.
Heat 3 tbsp oil until it smokes, then pour it directly over the chili pile — it should sizzle loudly. Toss immediately.
Dice the pork small and fry until dry, then add ginger, 1 tbsp soy and 1 tbsp vinegar and cook 5 minutes into a loose topping.
Soak the wood ear and dice with the dried tofu, carrot and potato. Simmer in 800 ml stock 10 minutes.
Season with soy, vinegar and chili flakes, stream in a beaten egg, and ladle over boiled noodles.
Soak the brisket 30 minutes, blanch, then simmer with ginger, star anise and peppercorn 2 hours. The broth should be clear — skim often and never boil hard.
Slice the cooked beef thin. Simmer daikon slices in the broth 10 minutes.
Cook the noodles in a separate pot, transfer to bowls, ladle over the clear broth, and top with beef, daikon, scallion, cilantro and chili oil.
Make a very stiff dough with 500 g flour and 200 ml water. Knead 15 minutes and rest 30 minutes — stiff dough is what makes the shards hold.
Fry diced pork and tomato into a simple sauce with soy and a splash of water.
Hold the dough over boiling water and shave thin strips straight into the pot with a knife. Cook 2 minutes, drain, and top with the sauce.
Fry pork belly slices until the fat renders, then add green beans and garlic and cook 3 minutes.
Add 1 tbsp light soy, 1 tsp dark soy and 250 ml water, bring to a boil.
Lay fresh noodles loosely over the vegetables, cover, and steam 12 minutes on low. Lift the lid, toss everything together, and cook off any excess liquid.
Simmer diced beef with ginger 40 minutes in 1.5 litres water.
Add shredded dried tofu, soaked wood ear and glass noodles, and cook 8 minutes.
Thicken with cornstarch slurry until it is thick enough to hold a spoon upright, then season hard with white pepper (2 tsp), soy and vinegar. Finish with sesame oil.
Salt and squeeze the cabbage, mix with pork, scallion and soy, and fill the wrappers.
Build the bowl: 2 tbsp black vinegar, 1 tbsp chili oil, 1 tbsp light soy, 1 tsp sugar, a pinch of dried shrimp and minced garlic. Add 150 ml hot water.
Boil the dumplings 6 minutes and slide them into the bowl with a little cooking water.
Cut the pork into 5 cm squares and blanch 5 minutes. Tie each square with twine so it holds shape.
Line a clay pot with a thick layer of scallion and ginger — this is what stops the skin scorching. Sit the pork skin-down on top.
Pour in 300 ml shaoxing wine, 3 tbsp light soy, 1 tbsp dark soy and 3 tbsp sugar. Simmer 2 hours on the lowest heat, then flip skin-up and steam 30 minutes.
Score the fish along the spine and rub with shaoxing wine. Poach in barely simmering water with ginger 6 minutes — the water must never boil or the skin tears.
Lift the fish onto a plate and keep warm.
Simmer 4 tbsp black vinegar, 4 tbsp sugar, 2 tbsp soy, 100 ml poaching water and ginger 2 minutes, thicken with cornstarch, and pour over the fish.
Blanch the shoots 5 minutes to remove the bitterness, then cut into rolling chunks.
Fry them in 3 tbsp oil over medium heat 6 minutes until the edges turn gold and slightly dry.
Add 2 tbsp soy, 2 tbsp sugar and 100 ml water. Cover and braise 8 minutes, then reduce until the sauce is syrupy. Finish with sesame oil.
Mix 600 g pork with 1 egg, chopped water chestnut, ginger, scallion, 1 tbsp soy, 2 tbsp cornstarch and 4 tbsp water. Stir hard 3 minutes until it becomes a sticky paste.
Shape into 4 large balls — larger is better here — and fry in 170°C oil until browned, about 5 minutes.
Line a clay pot with cabbage leaves, sit the meatballs on top, add soy, sugar and water to half-cover, and simmer 60 minutes.
Cut 6 scallions into 5 cm lengths. Warm 100 ml oil over low heat, add the scallions, and fry gently 10 minutes until dark brown and crisp — rushing this makes them bitter.
Add 3 tbsp soy and 1 tbsp sugar to the scallion oil and simmer 1 minute.
Boil the noodles, drain well, and toss with 2 tbsp of the scallion oil. Top with the fried scallions.
Poach the chicken thighs with ginger and scallion 15 minutes, then plunge into ice water to tighten the skin.
Mix 300 ml shaoxing wine, 200 ml chicken poaching liquid, 1 tsp salt and 1 tsp sugar.
Submerge the chicken and refrigerate at least 6 hours. Slice cold and serve with a spoon of the wine liquid.
Blanch the duck 5 minutes, then dry it thoroughly — wet skin will not take color.
Sear the duck in a dry pot until the skin renders and browns. Add ginger, scallion, star anise, 3 tbsp light soy, 2 tbsp dark soy and 3 tbsp sugar.
Pour in shaoxing wine and water to half-cover. Braise 70 minutes, turning every 15 minutes, then reduce the liquid to a lacquer and spoon it over.
Soak the rice cakes in warm water 20 minutes until they bend without snapping. Separate them.
Fry pork and shiitake 2 minutes, add the cabbage and cook until it softens.
Add the rice cakes, 2 tbsp soy, 1 tbsp oyster sauce and 100 ml water. Toss gently 4 minutes until they turn tender and the sauce is absorbed.
Soak the glutinous rice 2 hours and drain. Cut one end off the lotus root and pack the rice into the holes with a chopstick, tapping as you go.
Replace the cap and secure with toothpicks. Cover with water, add 150 g sugar and simmer 90 minutes.
Let it cool entirely in the syrup — this is what turns the slices glossy and deep amber. Slice and spoon syrup over.
Peel and devein the shrimp, then dry them thoroughly. Toss with salt, egg white and 2 tsp cornstarch — this velvet coating keeps them tender.
Chill 20 minutes, then blanch in 120°C oil for 30 seconds. They should just turn opaque.
Stir-fry scallion 15 seconds, return the shrimp, and season with a pinch of salt and a drop of sesame oil. Nothing else.
Dice the sausage, carrot and cooked shrimp small. Use cold rice broken into loose grains.
Scramble the eggs in a hot wok until barely set, add the rice and press it flat for 30 seconds before tossing.
Add all the diced ingredients and toss 2 minutes. Season with salt and white pepper only — soy sauce would darken it and clouds the look.
Rub the duck all over with 3 tbsp salt mixed with crushed star anise, and refrigerate 2 hours — this firms the meat.
Rinse off the salt, put the duck in cold water with ginger and scallion, and bring to 90°C. Hold there 25 minutes, never boiling.
Turn off the heat and leave the duck in the liquid 40 minutes. Chill before chopping; serve at room temperature.
Boil 500 ml water with a pinch of salt. In the serving bowl, put 1 tbsp soy, 1 tsp oil, a pinch of sugar and chopped scallion.
Ladle 200 ml hot water into the bowl to make the broth.
Cook the noodles 2 minutes, lift them into the bowl, and top with a few drops of sesame oil.
Pound the pork cutlets thin with the back of a knife, then marinate 15 minutes with soy, shaoxing wine and a pinch of sugar. Dust with cornstarch.
Fry in 3 tbsp oil 3 minutes per side until browned and just cooked. Rest and slice.
Cook the noodles and greens, put them in a bowl with 1 tbsp soy and hot water, and lay the pork on top.
Soak the preserved greens 10 minutes to pull out excess salt, then squeeze and chop.
Slice the pork thin and stir-fry 1 minute, add the greens and 1 tsp sugar, and cook 2 minutes until fragrant.
Add 400 ml water, simmer 3 minutes, and ladle over cooked noodles.
Slice the pork thin, the bamboo shoots even thinner. Soak and chop the greens.
Stir-fry the pork 1 minute, add bamboo shoots and greens and cook 2 minutes with a splash of shaoxing wine.
Add 500 ml water and 1 tbsp soy, simmer 4 minutes, then pour over noodles boiled separately.
Blanch the pork 3 minutes and cut into chunks. Blanch the bamboo shoots 5 minutes to tame the bitterness.
Fry ginger and scallion, add the pork and render 4 minutes, then 2 tbsp light soy, 1 tsp dark soy and 2 tbsp sugar.
Add the shoots, shaoxing wine and water to cover. Simmer 50 minutes, then reduce until the sauce is thick and dark.
Blanch the beef 5 minutes and rinse. Fry onion, ginger and star anise 3 minutes until soft.
Add the beef and brown, then 3 tbsp light soy, 1 tbsp dark soy, 1 tbsp sugar and water to cover. Simmer 60 minutes.
Add potato and carrot and cook 25 minutes more, until the potato edges soften and thicken the sauce.
Blanch the brisket 5 minutes, rinse, and cut into chunks.
Fry onion and ginger until soft, add half the tomatoes and cook 6 minutes until they break down into a sauce.
Add the beef, 2 tbsp soy, 1 tsp sugar and water to cover. Simmer 70 minutes, then add the rest of the tomatoes for the last 20 minutes so you get both body and fresh pieces.
Chop the chicken into pieces and marinate 20 minutes with oyster sauce, soy, ginger, cornstarch and shaoxing wine.
Fry the shiitake slices 2 minutes until they smell nutty
Add the chicken and fry 5 minutes, then 100 ml water, cover, and simmer 10 minutes until the sauce thickens around the chicken.
Score the wings twice on each side so the glaze penetrates. Pat dry.
Fry them in oil 4 minutes per side until golden, then add ginger, garlic and star anise for 30 seconds.
Add 2 tbsp light soy, 1 tsp dark soy, 1 tbsp sugar and 200 ml water. Simmer 15 minutes, then reduce until sticky.
Split the shrimp along the back and devein, keeping the shells on for flavor.
Fry half the minced garlic in 2 tbsp oil over low heat until pale gold, then add the rest of the garlic raw — this gives two layers of garlic flavor.
Add the shrimp and toss 2 minutes, splash in 1 tbsp soy and a pinch of sugar, and finish with scallion.
Julienne the potato into 2 mm shreds and soak in cold water 10 minutes, changing the water once — this rinses off the starch so they stay crisp.
Dry them well. Fry dried chilies and garlic in a smoking wok 15 seconds.
Add the potato and toss 90 seconds over the highest heat, splash 2 tbsp vinegar down the side, season with salt, and serve immediately.
Peel the pumpkin and cut into 3 cm wedges, removing the seeds and stringy core.
Arrange skin-down in a shallow dish and sprinkle with 1 tbsp sugar.
Steam 15 minutes until a chopstick slides through the flesh. Spoon the collected syrup back over before serving.
Cut the eggplant into rolls, salt 10 minutes, squeeze dry, and dust lightly with cornstarch — this stops it drinking all the oil.
Pan-fry in 3 tbsp oil 5 minutes until soft and browned on the edges.
Add garlic, 2 tbsp soy, 1 tbsp oyster sauce, 1 tsp sugar and 100 ml water. Simmer 4 minutes and thicken.
Halve the eggplants lengthwise and score the flesh in a crosshatch without cutting the skin.
Steam 12 minutes until completely soft and collapsed.
Fry minced garlic in 2 tbsp oil 30 seconds, add 1 tbsp soy and a pinch of sugar, spoon over the eggplant, and finish with scallion and chili oil.
Press the whole peppers flat with the side of a knife so they make good contact with the pan.
Dry-fry them in a hot pan 5 minutes, pressing, until the skin blisters and chars in patches.
Add 1 tbsp oil, garlic and 1 tbsp doubanjiang, then 1 tbsp soy, 1 tbsp vinegar and 1 tsp sugar. Toss 1 minute.
Smash the cucumber with the flat of a knife until it splits, then break into rough chunks — the cracked surface absorbs dressing far better than slices.
Salt 5 minutes and pour off the water that beads out.
Toss with mashed garlic, 2 tbsp black vinegar, 1 tbsp soy, 1 tsp sugar and sesame oil. Serve cold.
Soak the wood ear in warm water 20 minutes until fully expanded. Trim the hard knobs and tear into bite-size pieces.
Blanch 90 seconds in boiling water, then shock in ice water — this keeps them crunchy.
Toss with garlic, 2 tbsp vinegar, 1 tbsp soy, 1 tsp sugar, sesame oil and cilantro.
Rinse the kelp well and cut into thin shreds. Blanch 3 minutes — raw kelp is unpleasantly tough.
Drain and cool under running water.
Toss with garlic, 2 tbsp vinegar, 1 tbsp soy, 1 tsp sugar, chili oil and sesame oil. Rest 15 minutes before serving.
Blanch the spinach 20 seconds in boiling water, then plunge into ice water to keep the color. Squeeze out excess water.
Crush the peanuts lightly so they hold the dressing.
Toss with garlic, 1 tbsp rice vinegar, 1 tsp soy, a pinch of sugar and sesame oil.
Wash the spinach thoroughly and shake off the water, but do not dry it completely — the residual water helps it steam.
Fry sliced garlic in hot oil 20 seconds until fragrant and just pale gold.
Add the spinach and toss 60 seconds over high heat until just wilted. Salt at the end so it does not release water too early.
Cut the water spinach into 6 cm lengths, keeping stems and leaves separate.
Fry garlic and a pinch of chili flakes in a very hot wok 20 seconds.
Add the stems for 45 seconds, then the leaves for 45 seconds. Salt and serve at once — it wilts fast.
Rinse the sprouts and drain very well — wet sprouts steam instead of frying.
Fry garlic in a smoking wok 15 seconds, add the sprouts and toss 90 seconds over the highest heat.
Add the chives, 1 tbsp soy and a splash of vinegar, toss 20 seconds, and salt.
Trim the ends of the snow peas and pull off the string. Blanch 30 seconds in salted boiling water.
Marinate the shrimp with salt, white pepper and 1 tsp cornstarch, then sear 60 seconds and remove.
Fry garlic 15 seconds, add the peas and toss 1 minute, return the shrimp, season with a little oyster sauce.
Cut the celery on a sharp diagonal into 4 cm pieces. If the stalks are thick, peel the stringy outer layer.
Slice the pork thin and marinate 10 minutes with soy and cornstarch.
Stir-fry the pork 1 minute, add garlic and celery, and toss 2 minutes. The celery should still squeak when bitten.
Slice the beef across the grain and marinate 15 minutes with soy, cornstarch, a splash of water and 1 tsp oil.
Slice the onion into thick wedges and separate the layers.
Sear the beef in a smoking wok 45 seconds and remove. Fry the onion 2 minutes until translucent at the edges, return the beef with oyster sauce and black pepper, toss 30 seconds.
Cut the tofu into 2 cm slabs and pat dry. Pan-fry 3 minutes per side until golden — dry tofu does not stick.
Fry sliced shiitake 3 minutes until they release their aroma and start to brown.
Add 2 tbsp oyster sauce, 1 tbsp soy, 1 tsp sugar and 150 ml water, slide the tofu back in, and simmer 5 minutes. Thicken lightly.
Cut the tofu into triangles or thick squares and blot dry with paper.
Fry in 2 tbsp oil 3 minutes per side until a golden crust forms; this keeps it from breaking in the sauce.
Add garlic, 2 tbsp soy, 1 tsp dark soy, 1 tsp sugar and 150 ml water. Simmer 5 minutes, thicken with cornstarch, and finish with scallion.
Blanch the ribs 3 minutes in boiling water, then rinse each one — this is what keeps the broth clear instead of grey.
Simmer the ribs with ginger in 1.5 litres water for 45 minutes, skimming any foam that rises.
Add peeled winter melon chunks and cook 15 minutes until translucent. Salt at the end, and finish with scallion.
Blanch the ribs 3 minutes and rinse. Cut the corn into thick wheels and the carrot into chunks.
Simmer ribs and ginger 40 minutes, then add corn and carrot.
Cook 25 minutes more. The corn sweetens the broth, so salt only at the very end.
Blanch and rinse the ribs, then simmer with ginger 45 minutes.
Peel the yam wearing gloves — its sap irritates skin — and cut into 4 cm lengths.
Add the yam for the last 20 minutes only; overcooked yam dissolves and turns the soup cloudy.
Blanch the ribs 3 minutes and rinse. Peel the lotus root and cut into thick rounds.
Simmer everything with ginger for 70 minutes. Use a heavy pot and keep it at a bare simmer.
The lotus should be soft enough to cut with a spoon. Salt at the end.
Tear the seaweed into small pieces and put it in the serving bowl with a pinch of salt and a drop of sesame oil.
Bring 600 ml water to a boil with dried shrimp if using.
Stream in 2 beaten eggs while stirring once, pour straight over the seaweed, and finish with scallion.
Cut the silken tofu into 1 cm cubes and slide them into 700 ml simmering stock.
Season with salt and white pepper, then thicken with 2 tbsp cornstarch slurry so the tofu stays suspended.
Stream in a beaten egg, turn off the heat, and finish with scallion and sesame oil.
Use skin-on bone-in chicken for body. Blanch 2 minutes, then rinse off the scum.
Simmer with ginger and scallion in 1.5 litres water at the barest bubble for 75 minutes. Skim whenever foam appears.
Salt only at the end. A hard boil emulsifies the fat and turns the broth milky.
Chop the duck into pieces and blanch 5 minutes to remove the gaminess. Rinse well.
Simmer with ginger in 2 litres water for 90 minutes, skimming often.
Add yam for the last 25 minutes. Season with salt and white pepper; a single star anise is enough.
Slice the fish thin and marinate 10 minutes with salt, white pepper and 1 tbsp cornstarch.
Fry tomato wedges in 1 tbsp oil 5 minutes until they collapse into a sauce, then add 700 ml water and ginger.
Simmer 8 minutes, slide in the fish slices, and poach 90 seconds. Do not stir — swirl the pot instead.
Mix the pork with ginger, scallion, 1 tbsp cornstarch, 1 egg white and salt. Stir in one direction until sticky, then chill 15 minutes.
Bring 1 litre water to a gentle simmer. Scoop small balls with a wet spoon and drop them in; they are done when they float.
Add thin winter melon slices for 6 minutes, then season and finish with sesame oil.
Slice the liver thin and rinse under cold water until it stops bleeding. Marinate 10 minutes with ginger, salt, shaoxing wine and cornstarch.
Bring 700 ml water to a boil, add the liver and cook 60 seconds only — longer turns it grainy.
Add the spinach for 30 seconds, season, and finish with sesame oil.
Scramble 2 eggs in a hot wok and remove while still soft.
Fry tomato wedges 4 minutes until they release their juice, add 600 ml water and a pinch of sugar, and simmer 5 minutes.
Return the eggs, cook the noodles separately, and pour the sauce over. Finish with scallion.
Mix the pork with ginger, scallion, 1 tbsp soy, 1 tsp sesame oil and 2 tbsp water. Stir until sticky.
Fill and fold the wrappers, pinching firmly so they do not open in the water.
Bring 1 litre light stock to a simmer. Cook the wontons 3 minutes, add greens for 30 seconds, and season the broth with soy, sesame oil and white pepper.
Simmer beef brisket with star anise and garlic 70 minutes, then slice it. Keep the broth.
Soak the rice noodles in hot water 5 minutes until soft, then blanch 30 seconds.
Put the noodles in a bowl, ladle over hot broth, and top with beef, crushed peanuts, chili oil and scallion.
Soak the rice noodles 15 minutes until flexible, drain, and cut shorter.
Stir-fry shrimp 1 minute and remove. Scramble the egg and remove.
Fry onion and 1 tbsp curry powder 40 seconds, add noodles and toss 2 minutes, then return shrimp and egg with sprouts and soy.
Fry onion, garlic and 2 tbsp curry powder in 2 tbsp oil over low heat 2 minutes — blooming the spice in fat is what makes the flavor deep instead of dusty.
Add chicken pieces and brown, then potato and carrot.
Pour in 300 ml water and simmer 20 minutes, then stir in 150 ml coconut milk and season. Do not boil hard after the coconut goes in.
Blanch the beef 5 minutes and rinse. Fry onion and garlic 3 minutes, then stir in 2 tbsp curry powder for 40 seconds.
Add the beef, 600 ml water and simmer covered 60 minutes.
Add potato and carrot and cook 25 minutes more. Stir in coconut milk at the end and season.
Brown chicken pieces in oil 5 minutes and remove.
Fry onion, garlic, ginger and 1 tbsp curry powder 3 minutes, then return the chicken.
Pour in 250 ml coconut milk and simmer 15 minutes until slightly thickened. Season with salt and a pinch of sugar.
Blanch the beef 5 minutes, rinse, and cut into chunks.
Fry ginger, scallion, star anise and dried chilies, add the beef and brown, then 3 tbsp light soy, 1 tbsp dark soy and 1 tbsp sugar.
Add shaoxing wine and water to cover, simmer 85 minutes, then reduce the sauce until it coats the meat.
Blanch the ribs 3 minutes and dry them.
Caramelize 1 tbsp sugar in oil until amber, add the ribs and turn to coat, then ginger, star anise and shaoxing wine.
Add 2 tbsp light soy, 1 tsp dark soy and water to cover. Simmer 35 minutes, then reduce until sticky.
Cut the chicken into chunks, marinate 10 minutes with salt and soy, then coat in beaten egg and cornstarch.
Fry at 170°C for 4 minutes, rest, then fry again at 190°C for 60 seconds.
Stir-fry pepper and onion 1 minute, add 3 tbsp sugar, 3 tbsp vinegar, 1 tbsp soy and 4 tbsp water, thicken, and fold in the chicken off the heat.
Cut the chicken into chunks, coat in beaten egg then cornstarch, and fry at 175°C for 4 minutes until crisp.
Fry dried chilies, garlic and ginger in 1 tbsp oil 30 seconds.
Add 3 tbsp sugar, 2 tbsp vinegar, 2 tbsp soy and 100 ml water, simmer 2 minutes until syrupy, then toss the chicken in it just before serving.
Cut the chicken into chunks, coat in egg and cornstarch, and fry at 175°C for 4 minutes.
Zest one orange and juice it. Fry garlic and ginger 20 seconds, add the juice, zest, 3 tbsp sugar, 2 tbsp rice vinegar and 1 tbsp soy.
Reduce 2 minutes until glossy, then toss the chicken through off the heat.
Slice the beef thin and marinate 15 minutes with soy, cornstarch and 1 tbsp water.
Blanch the broccoli 90 seconds in salted water, then drain — this keeps it bright and cuts the wok time.
Sear the beef 45 seconds, add garlic, return the broccoli with 2 tbsp oyster sauce and 3 tbsp water, and toss 1 minute.
Beat 4 eggs with salt and white pepper. Fold in chopped shrimp, sprouts and scallion — do not overmix, or it turns dense.
Ladle into a hot oiled pan as small rounds and cook 2 minutes per side until puffed and golden.
Serve with a quick gravy: 100 ml stock, 1 tbsp soy, 1 tsp cornstarch, simmered 1 minute.
Boil the noodles 1 minute short, drain, rinse cold and toss with oil.
Stir-fry sliced chicken 3 minutes, then add onion, cabbage and carrot and cook 2 minutes.
Add the noodles, 2 tbsp soy and 1 tbsp oyster sauce, and toss over high heat 2 minutes until the edges crisp.
Mix the pork with ginger, scallion, soy and sesame oil. Keep the filling small — about a teaspoon.
Fold into triangles and press out all the air, or they burst in the oil.
Fry at 170°C for 3 minutes until golden and blistered. Serve with vinegar and chili oil.
Beat 3 eggs with 1.5 times their volume of warm water and a pinch of salt. Strain through a sieve — this removes the foam that causes pockmarks.
Pour into a shallow bowl, cover with a plate, and steam over gentle heat 10 minutes.
Lay marinated shrimp on top and steam 3 minutes more. Drizzle soy and sesame oil, scatter scallion.
Blanch the spinach 20 seconds and drain, then arrange in a shallow bowl.
Fry whole garlic cloves in 1 tbsp oil 3 minutes until golden, add 400 ml stock and diced century egg.
Simmer 5 minutes, season, and pour over the spinach.
Soak the glass noodles 10 minutes and spread them in a shallow dish.
Lay cabbage leaves on top. Fry minced garlic in 3 tbsp oil until pale gold, mix with 2 tbsp soy and 1 tsp oyster sauce, and spoon over.
Steam 12 minutes, then scatter scallion and chili flakes and pour a final spoon of hot oil over.
Peel the daikon and cut into 3 cm rounds, then score a shallow cross in each face so the sauce penetrates.
Fry ginger and star anise 30 seconds, add the daikon and brown 3 minutes.
Add 2 tbsp light soy, 1 tsp dark soy, 1 tbsp sugar and 300 ml water. Simmer 20 minutes until the radish turns translucent.
Peel the melon and cut into thick blocks, scoring the surface in a crosshatch.
Fry garlic 20 seconds, add the melon and sear 3 minutes until the edges brown.
Add 1 tbsp soy, 1 tbsp oyster sauce, 1 tsp sugar and 200 ml water. Simmer 12 minutes until tender and glossy.
Peel the lotus root and slice 3 mm thick. Soak in water with a splash of vinegar to stop it browning.
Blanch 60 seconds, then drain very well.
Stir-fry garlic and chili 20 seconds, add the slices and toss 2 minutes, splash vinegar and salt, and finish with scallion.
Soak the kelp 30 minutes to remove excess salt, then cut into wide ribbons and blanch 3 minutes.
Blanch the pork 3 minutes, cut into chunks, and fry with ginger and star anise until browned.
Add soy sauces, sugar and shaoxing wine with water to cover. Simmer 50 minutes, add the kelp, and cook 20 minutes more.
Cut the celery on the diagonal and the dried tofu into thin strips.
Blanch the celery 40 seconds so it stays green and crisp.
Fry garlic and chili 20 seconds, add the tofu and fry 2 minutes, then the celery with soy sauce for 1 minute.
Rinse 2 cups rice and add water to the normal line. Slice the sausage on the diagonal and the shiitake thick.
Lay sausage, shiitake and carrot on top of the rice — do not stir them in, or they sink and steam instead of roast.
Cook on the normal cycle. When it finishes, rest 10 minutes, then fluff with 1 tbsp soy, 1 tsp dark soy and scallion.
Soak the red beans overnight. Drain and cover with 1.5 litres fresh water.
Simmer 60 minutes until the beans split and the liquid darkens. Keep the pot at a low burble.
Add 4 tbsp sugar in the last 10 minutes only — sugar added early stops the beans softening. Serve hot or chilled.
Soak the rice cakes in warm water 20 minutes until they bend.
Simmer 800 ml stock with sliced pork and cabbage 6 minutes.
Add the rice cakes and cook 4 minutes until tender but still chewy. Season with soy, salt and sesame oil.
Rinse 1 cup rice and simmer in 1.5 litres water 30 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Add peeled pumpkin cubes and cook 15 minutes until they collapse.
Mash roughly for texture, sweeten to taste, and stir in a splash of milk if you want it creamier.
Simmer 1 cup rice in 2 litres water with sliced ginger for 45 minutes until the grains break down.
Poach the chicken breast 12 minutes in the congee, then lift out and shred with two forks.
Return the chicken, season with salt and white pepper, and finish with scallion and sesame oil.
Rinse the rice and simmer in 1.5 litres water 25 minutes.
Add peeled sweet potato chunks and cook 15 minutes until they soften and sweeten the liquid.
Stir gently — the sweet potato should stay in pieces, not dissolve completely.
